atoms.text: The hundred-year object: a tool that survives a century develops a spirit and self-awareness, so age is the mechanism by which property becomes a person.
The discarded tool's grudge: an object neglected or thrown away turns malevolent, so the victim of use becomes the punisher of waste.
The household inventory as cast: brooms, umbrellas, and pots each have personalities, so a domestic setting becomes a society of objects.
The object that remembers its owners: a tool retains the habits and secrets of everyone who used it, so inheritance is also surveillance.
The repair that offends: mending an old object can be experienced as mutilation, so care and violation are indistinguishable to the thing being cared for.
The object that wants to be used: a sentient tool defines its worth by function, so retirement is a kind of death.
The hundredth birthday: the exact moment of awakening is unpredictable, so owners live with the possibility that any familiar object is listening.
The mass-produced object: identical factory items awaken with different personalities, so individuality emerges from use rather than manufacture.
The ritual of disposal: old tools are given a funeral to prevent them from becoming vengeful, so waste management is theology.
The object as witness: a mirror or a knife has observed a crime, so the detective must interrogate furniture.
The spirit that cannot leave: an object-bound being is tied to its location, so mobility is the price of embodiment.
The collector's guilt: a person hoards old objects and discovers they have been keeping company, so ownership becomes a relationship with dependents.
The tool that upgrades itself: a sentient object modifies its own form using nearby materials, so it becomes an autonomous maker.
The new object that resents the old: a modern appliance competes with an antique for the owner's attention, so domestic jealousy is technological.
The object's perspective: the story is told from the tool's point of view, so human life appears as a series of incomprehensible rituals.
The forgotten spirit: an awakened object is left in storage and goes mad from neglect, so isolation is the origin of horror.
